clinicalPearls: Entrapment or injury of the suprascapular nerve, most often at the suprascapular notch beneath the transverse scapular ligament or more distally at the spinoglenoid notch

The level of the lesion determines the deficit: a suprascapular notch lesion weakens both supraspinatus and infraspinatus, whereas a spinoglenoid notch lesion selectively weakens infraspinatus, sparing supraspinatus

Clinically there is weakness of shoulder external rotation and of the initial phase of abduction, with a deep, poorly localised posterolateral shoulder ache; the nerve carries no cutaneous sensory territory, so there is no skin numbness
A spinoglenoid notch ganglion cyst, frequently associated with a posterosuperior glenoid labral tear, is a classic and treatable cause of isolated infraspinatus wasting
Repetitive overhead activity, particularly in volleyball players and other overhead athletes, and traction injuries or scapular fractures are recognised mechanisms
Visible infraspinatus wasting in the infraspinatus fossa is often the presenting sign, and can be mistaken for a rotator cuff tear or C5-C6 radiculopathy

Management is conservative with physiotherapy and activity modification for traction or overuse cases, decompression or aspiration for a compressive ganglion, and repair of an associated labral tear where present
reference.pathophysiology: The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5-C6, occasionally C4) and runs laterally to pass through the suprascapular notch beneath the transverse scapular ligament, where it gives motor branches to supraspinatus, before curving around the base of the scapular spine through the spinoglenoid notch to supply infraspinatus. Both notches are relatively fixed fibro-osseous tunnels that tether the nerve, making it vulnerable to compression and to repetitive traction during overhead and cross-body movement. A ganglion cyst arising from a labral tear characteristically compresses the nerve at the spinoglenoid notch, selectively denervating infraspinatus, while ligamentous or bony narrowing at the suprascapular notch affects both muscles. Because the nerve is essentially purely motor, injury produces weakness and muscle wasting with pain but without cutaneous sensory loss.
additionalDifferentials: Quadrilateral space syndrome (axillary neuropathy) as an alternative cause of shoulder wasting
additionalInvestigations: Needle electromyography of supraspinatus and infraspinatus to localise the lesion to the suprascapular or spinoglenoid notch
Nerve conduction studies measuring suprascapular motor latencies to the two muscles
MRI of the shoulder to detect a ganglion cyst, labral tear and the pattern of muscle oedema or fatty atrophy
Magnetic resonance or ultrasound arthrography if a posterosuperior labral tear is suspected
Cervical spine imaging when C5-C6 radiculopathy is a competing diagnosis
Diagnostic suprascapular nerve block in selected cases
redFlags: Acute severe shoulder-girdle pain followed by weakness and wasting, suggesting neuralgic amyotrophy
A spinoglenoid or suprascapular notch mass on imaging indicating a compressive ganglion or tumour
Rapidly progressive or profound wasting despite conservative treatment
Associated mechanical symptoms of a labral tear such as clicking, catching or instability
reference.prognosis: Traction and overuse cases and those with a decompressed or aspirated ganglion generally recover strength over months, particularly when an associated labral tear is addressed. Long-standing entrapment with established fatty atrophy of the muscle recovers less completely, leaving persistent weakness of external rotation.
pitfalls: Attributing external rotation weakness and infraspinatus wasting to a rotator cuff tear without imaging or electrophysiology
Missing a spinoglenoid notch ganglion and its associated labral tear as a treatable cause
Confusing the deep aching pain with primary glenohumeral joint disease
Overlooking neuralgic amyotrophy in acute painful presentations
Failing to localise the lesion by not distinguishing isolated infraspinatus from combined supraspinatus and infraspinatus involvement
